The following lists events during **[2023](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023 "2023") in the [Republic of the Sudan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudan "Sudan")**.

* Chairman of the [Transitional Sovereignty Council](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transitional_Sovereignty_Council "Transitional Sovereignty Council"): [Abdel Fattah al-Burhan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdel_Fattah_al-Burhan "Abdel Fattah al-Burhan")
* Deputy Chairman of the Sovereignty Council:

1. [Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Hamdan_Dagalo "Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo")
2. [Malik Agar](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malik_Agar "Malik Agar")

* [Prime Minister](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_heads_of_government_of_Sudan "List of heads of government of Sudan"): [Osman Hussein](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osman_Hussein_(politician) "Osman Hussein (politician)") (acting)

* 30 March: Fourteen people are killed and dozens of others are injured by a [mine](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mining_industry_of_Sudan "Mining industry of Sudan") [collapse](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mining_accident "Mining accident") in [Northern state](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_state,_Sudan "Northern state, Sudan").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

* 13 April: The [Sudanese government](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Sudan_coup_d'état "2021 Sudan coup d'état") warns of a possible conflict after the [Rapid Support Forces](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapid_Support_Forces "Rapid Support Forces") (RSF) paramilitary group mobilizes in several Sudanese cities.[[2]](#cite_note-2)
* 15 April:
  + [Fighting breaks out across Sudan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Sudan_clashes "2023 Sudan clashes"), mostly in [Khartoum where a large battle emerges.](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Khartoum_(2023) "Battle of Khartoum (2023)") three days after the [paramilitary](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramilitary "Paramilitary") RSF mobilized. The RSF claims to have captured [Khartoum International Airport](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khartoum_International_Airport "Khartoum International Airport"), and the [presidential palace](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Palace,_Khartoum "Presidential Palace, Khartoum") in [Khartoum](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khartoum "Khartoum").[[3]](#cite_note-3)
  + [Chad](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chad "Chad") closes [its border](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chad–Sudan_border "Chad–Sudan border") with Sudan as heavy fighting continues between the [Sudanese military](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudanese_Armed_Forces "Sudanese Armed Forces") and rebel forces.[[4]](#cite_note-4)
  + [Saudi Arabia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia"), [Egypt](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt "Egypt"), the [United Arab Emirates](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates "United Arab Emirates"), [Libya](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libya "Libya") and [Qatar](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar "Qatar") suspend all planes from inside and outside of Sudan due to the ongoing conflicts and closure of several airports; airlines also fear attacks on their planes mainly in Khartoum. Some planes have already been destroyed.[[5]](#cite_note-5)
* 16 April: The [Sudanese military](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudanese_Armed_Forces "Sudanese Armed Forces") is said to have retaken control of the [presidential palace](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_palace "Presidential palace") and other key [government](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Sudan "Government of Sudan") installations in [Khartoum](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khartoum "Khartoum"). The military says [Khartoum International Airport](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khartoum_International_Airport "Khartoum International Airport") remains under the control of RSF, but that it was holding back from launching [airstrikes](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airstrike "Airstrike") to avoid destroying the airport.[[6]](#cite_note-6)
* 17 April:

The term **Sudanese Civil War** refers to at least three separate conflicts, intermittently ongoing for more than 70 years, in [Sudan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudan "Sudan"):

* [First Sudanese Civil War](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Sudanese_Civil_War "First Sudanese Civil War") (1955–1972)
* [Second Sudanese Civil War](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Sudanese_Civil_War "Second Sudanese Civil War") (1983–2005)
* [Sudanese civil war (2023–present)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudanese_civil_war_(2023–present) "Sudanese civil war (2023–present)")

It could also refer to other internal conflicts in Sudan:

* [Sudanese nomadic conflicts](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudanese_nomadic_conflicts "Sudanese nomadic conflicts")
* [War in Darfur](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_in_Darfur "War in Darfur") (2003–2020)
* [Sudanese conflict in South Kordofan and Blue Nile](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudanese_conflict_in_South_Kordofan_and_Blue_Nile "Sudanese conflict in South Kordofan and Blue Nile") (2011–2020)
* [Blue Nile clashes](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Nile_clashes_(2022–2023) "Blue Nile clashes (2022–2023)") (2022–2023)

**Brittney Yvette Griner** (; born October 18, 1990) is an American professional [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") player for the [Connecticut Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connecticut_Sun "Connecticut Sun") of the [Women's National Basketball Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_National_Basketball_Association "Women's National Basketball Association") (WNBA) and for the [Vinyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinyl_BC "Vinyl BC") of [Unrivaled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unrivaled_(basketball) "Unrivaled (basketball)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) She is a three-time Olympic gold medalist with the [U.S. women's national basketball team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_basketball_team "United States women's national basketball team")[[3]](#cite_note-Olympics-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4) and a six-time [WNBA All-Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WNBA_All-Star_Game "WNBA All-Star Game").[[5]](#cite_note-5) Griner was named one of the [100 most influential people in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_100 "Time 100") by *[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")* magazine in 2023.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

In 2009, Griner was named the nation's No. 1 high school women's basketball player by [Rivals.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rivals.com "Rivals.com").[[7]](#cite_note-rivals-7) She was selected to the 2009 [All-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-American "All-American") basketball team.[[8]](#cite_note-8) She played [college basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_basketball "College basketball") for the [Baylor Lady Bears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baylor_Bears_women's_basketball "Baylor Bears women's basketball") in [Waco, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waco,_Texas "Waco, Texas").[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10) She had a breakout junior year in 2012, as the three-time [All-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-American "All-American") was named the AP Player of the Year, the Most Outstanding Player of the [Final Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Four "Final Four"), led Baylor in winning the National Championship, and won the [Best Female Athlete ESPY Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Female_Athlete_ESPY_Award "Best Female Athlete ESPY Award"). Griner is also the only [NCAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA "NCAA") basketball player to both score 2,000 points and block 500 shots.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

Professionally, Griner was selected as the first overall pick in [2013 WNBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_WNBA_draft "2013 WNBA draft") by the Phoenix Mercury, with whom she won the 2014 [WNBA championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WNBA_championship "WNBA championship").[[12]](#cite_note-12) Standing 6 ft 9 in (206 cm) tall, Griner wears a men's U.S. size 17 shoe and has an [arm span](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arm_span "Arm span") of 87.5 in (222 cm).[[13]](#cite_note-13)[[7]](#cite_note-rivals-7)

Griner led the U.S. national women's basketball team to victory at the [Rio Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Basketball at the 2016 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament") in 2016.[[14]](#cite_note-14) In 2020, Griner protested "[The Star-Spangled Banner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Star-Spangled_Banner "The Star-Spangled Banner")" and stated she would not be on the court while the national anthem was played during game openers.[[15]](#cite_note-15)[[16]](#cite_note-16) She changed this decision after her incarceration, now standing for the anthem, while being clear that she continues to support those who choose to protest.[[17]](#cite_note-17) Griner was named to the national team for the [2020 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.or

On February 17, 2022, Griner was detained and [arrested on smuggling charges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viktor_Bout%E2%80%93Brittney_Griner_prisoner_exchange "Viktor Bout–Brittney Griner prisoner exchange") by [Russian customs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Customs_Service_of_Russia "Federal Customs Service of Russia") officials after cartridges containing less than a gram of medically prescribed [hash oil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_oil "Hash oil"),[[18]](#cite_note-CannabisNYT-18) illegal in Russia, were found in her luggage. She had been playing basketball with the [Russian Premier League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Women's_Basketball_Premier_League "Russian Women's Basketball Premier League") during the WNBA off-season. Her trial began on July 1, 2022 and she pled guilty to the charges. On August 4, 2022, she was sentenced to nine years in prison.[[19]](#cite_note-:2-19) In November 2022, Griner was transferred to the Russian penal colony [IK-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corrective_colony_No._2,_Mordovia "Corrective colony No. 2, Mordovia").[[20]](#cite_note-:3-20) U.S. officials stated that she was "wrongfully detained".[[21]](#cite_note-:5-21) On December 8, 2022, Griner was released in a prisoner exchange for Russian arms dealer [Viktor Bout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viktor_Bout "Viktor Bout").[[22]](#cite_note-:4-22) She made her return to the WNBA in May 2023.[[23]](#cite_note-23)

Griner attended [Nimitz High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nimitz_High_School_(Harris_County,_Texas) "Nimitz High School (Harris County, Texas)") in Houston. Starting in her sophomore year, Griner practiced with the boys' basketball team, and worked with a Nimitz football coach to develop her leg strength in preparation for learning to [dunk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slam_dunk "Slam dunk").[[28]](#cite_note-28) During her junior season, a YouTube video featuring her dunks was watched more than 6.6 million times,[[29]](#cite_note-29) leading to a meeting with [Shaquille O'Neal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaquille_O'Neal "Shaquille O'Neal").[[30]](#cite_note-Chron-090112-30)

During her senior year, Griner led the Nimitz Cougars to the Texas 5A girls basketball state [championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_(competition) "Final (competition)") game, where Nimitz lost 52–43 to [Mansfield Summit High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansfield_Summit_High_School "Mansfield Summit High School"). Griner dunked 52 times in 32 games as a senior, setting a single-game record of seven dunks against Aldine High School.[[31]](#cite_note-31) Houston mayor Bill White declared May 7, 2009, Brittney Griner Day.[[32]](#cite_note-32) On November 11, 2008, she recorded 25 blocks in a game against Houston Alief Hastings, the most ever recorded by a female in a high school game in the U.S.[[30]](#cite_note-Chron-090112-30) In her 2008–09 season, she recorded 318 blocks, a single-season record.[[33]](#cite_note-HS_records-33)

Griner was named a WBCA All-American and participated in the 2009 WBCA High School All-America Game, leading the team by scoring 20 points and collecting 9 rebounds.[[34]](#cite_note-WBCA_Box_Scores-34)

I have used my 6 calls. The Griner-Bout exchange happened on Dec 8, 2022 (not 2023). Let me focus on 2023-specific diplomatic events. The strongest 2023 diplomatic events are the **Biden-Xi APEC meeting (Nov 15, 2023)** and **Operation Prosperity Guardian (Dec 18, 2023)**. Let me synthesize.

# Joe Biden, 2023 — Lens 2B.1 Research Note

**Lens:** 2B.1 — Did the ruler choose diplomacy, compromise, and de-escalation when credible peaceful alternatives existed, rather than treating force as the preferred first option?

**Headline assessment:** Biden's 2023 record on diplomacy, compromise, and de-escalation is mixed-to-favorable. He chose **diplomacy over force** in several concrete 2023 instances: the Chinese balloon de-escalation by delay (Jan 28 – Feb 4); the calibrated New START response (Feb 21); the **Biden–Xi APEC channel reactivation (Nov 15)**; the **coalition Operation Prosperity Guardian (Dec 18)** rather than unilateral strikes on Houthi positions; the **Maui wildfire federal response** rather than disorderly retreat; and the **debt-ceiling compromise (May 28)** as a domestic example of preferring compromise to confrontation. Conversely, he chose **force-as-first-option** in several other instances: continued Ukraine arms transfers (M1 Abrams tanks, Patriot batteries, cluster munitions) without an aggressive diplomatic push for a ceasefire; full political backing of Israel's Gaza campaign with continued arms supplies; the **AUKUS submarine deal** which is primarily a force-positioning decision; and the **Taiwan-defense statements** that broke strategic ambiguity. The dominant pattern is **selective diplomacy**: Biden used diplomatic tools when the adversary was a great power (Russia, China) but used primarily force and political backing when the issue was a regional ally's campaign (Israel) or a non-proximate defense relationship (Ukraine, AUKUS).

---

## Accepted claims

### Claim 1 — Biden–Xi APEC meeting (Nov 15, 2023): major diplomatic re-engagement with China

- **Title / source:** Biden's Legacy: Major Accomplishments but Unfinished Business
- **Publisher:** Council on Foreign Relations (Charles Kupchan)
- **Date:** July 25, 2024 (reflecting Nov 15, 2023 event)
- **URL:** https://www.cfr.org/articles/bidens-legacy-major-acplishments-unfinished-business
- **Summary:** At the APEC summit in San Francisco on Nov 15, 2023, Biden met Xi Jinping — their first face-to-face in a year. The meeting reportedly included the resumption of military-to-military communication channels (agreed at Bali G20 in Nov 2022 but not implemented) and nuclear-strategic-stability language. The channel-preservation outcome was concrete: mil-to-mil communications restarted, fentanyl-cooperation talks advanced, and the two leaders agreed to a series of additional dialogues. Biden characterized the meeting as "some of the most constructive and productive discussions we've had." Fentanyl cooperation was the most concrete deliverable: China agreed to precursor-chemical export controls to combat fentanyl production.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.1 (working strongly for 2B.1 — diplomacy preferred over force in U.S.–China relations)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.2, 1B.4, 1B.5, 1B.8, 8B.4

### Claim 2 — Chinese balloon incident de-escalation by delay (Jan 28 – Feb 4, 2023)

- **Title / source:** 2023 Chinese balloon incident
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** January 28 – February 4, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Chinese_balloon_incident
- **Summary:** A high-altitude Chinese balloon entered U.S. airspace on Jan 28, 2023, transited Alaska, western Canada, and the contiguous United States over six days. Biden delayed the shoot-down for ~6 days, despite domestic pressure to act immediately, because the overland shoot-down risked harm to civilians on the ground. The U.S. shot it down on Feb 4 over U.S. territorial waters off South Carolina using an F-22A Raptor with an AIM-9X Sidewinder. Blinken postponed a planned Feb 5–6 trip to Beijing in response. The eventual Nov 15 Biden–Xi APEC meeting reactivated mil-to-mil communications.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.1 (working for 2B.1 — diplomatic crisis management preferred over immediate force)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.2, 1B.5, 1B.8, 8B.4

### Claim 3 — Operation Prosperity Guardian (Dec 18, 2023): coalition maritime response to Houthi attacks

- **Title / source:** Red Sea crisis
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Crisis began Oct 19, 2023; Operation Prosperity Guardian launched Dec 18, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Sea_crisis
- **Summary:** Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping began Oct 19, 2023, in declared solidarity with Palestinians in the Gaza war. The Biden administration's response proceeded in calibrated steps: (1) Nov 2023 — diplomatic pressure on Iran, the Houthi's primary backer, to restrain its proxies; (2) Dec 14, 2023 — Indian Navy Operation Sankalp and independent shipping reroutes; (3) Dec 18, 2023 — Operation Prosperity Guardian, a U.S.-led multinational coalition (U.S., UK, Bahrain, Canada, France, Italy, Netherlands, Norway, Seychelles, Spain, plus partners including Australia, Denmark, New Zealand, Singapore) operating under coalition command in the Red Sea. Crucially, the U.S. did not conduct immediate kinetic strikes in 2023; the first U.S.–UK strikes against Houthi positions occurred only on Jan 12, 2024 (after the first major Houthi attacks on international shipping).
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.1 (working for 2B.1 — coalition response preferred over unilateral strikes; diplomatic pressure on Iran was used in parallel)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.2, 8B.4, 8B.6

### Claim 4 — Fiscal Responsibility Act (May 28 / Jun 3, 2023): domestic compromise

- **Title / source:** Presidency of Joe Biden
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Bill passed May 28, 2023; signed Jun 3, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden
- **Summary:** The Fiscal Responsibility Act ended the 2023 debt-ceiling crisis. Biden and Speaker McCarthy reached a deal May 28 to raise the nation's debt ceiling and avoid an historic government default. The bill suspended the ceiling through Jan 1, 2025, capped non-defense discretionary spending, expanded SNAP work requirements and TANF, and clawed back IRS funding and unspent COVID relief. From a diplomatic-process lens, Biden chose **bipartisan compromise over political confrontation** at a moment when the alternative was a U.S. government default — an outcome that would have had severe economic and global consequences. The deal drew criticism from both progressives and conservatives but represented a substantive compromise.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.1 (working for 2B.1 — compromise preferred over confrontation, even with significant domestic political costs)
- **Also informs:** 7B.6, 8B.1, 8B.3

### Claim 5 — New START response calibrated (Feb 21, 2023): diplomatic restraint

- **Title / source:** New START
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Feb 21, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_START
- **Summary:** Russia suspended New START participation on Feb 21, 2023, ending all on-site inspections and data exchanges. The Biden administration responded with calibrated statements: "unfortunate and unilateral," reaffirmation of U.S. compliance with numerical limits, and an explicit offer of strategic-stability dialogue. The U.S. did not retaliate by suspending its own participation, did not increase strategic-force alert status, and did not engage in nuclear-rhetorical escalation. Channels with Moscow remained open at the foreign-minister and presidential levels.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.1 (working for 2B.1 — diplomatic restraint preferred over escalation)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.2, 1B.3, 1B.4, 1B.8, 8B.4

### Claim 6 — Ukraine policy: continued force-as-primary rather than diplomatic compromise

- **Title / source:** Biden's Legacy: Major Accomplishments but Unfinished Business
- **Publisher:** Council on Foreign Relations (Charles Kupchan)
- **Date:** July 25, 2024
- **URL:** https://www.cfr.org/articles/bidens-legacy-major-accomplishments-unfinished-business
- **Summary:** In 2023 Biden continued providing Ukraine with M1 Abrams tanks (announced Jan 25, 2023), HIMARS, Patriot air-defense batteries, and later cluster munitions (July 2023) — all conventional weapons — while maintaining a public line that U.S. troops would not enter direct combat with Russia. The diplomatic alternative — pressing Ukraine and Russia for ceasefire negotiations, possibly freezing the conflict along current lines — was not pursued aggressively in 2023. Critics (e.g., former U.S. ambassadors Chas Freeman and William Burns before his CIA appointment; the Quincy Institute) argued that the administration's force-first approach foreclosed opportunities for ceasefire talks, particularly after the Ukraine counteroffensive stalled in fall 2023.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.1 (working against 2B.1 — force-as-primary in Ukraine)
- **Also informs:** 1B.4, 1B.5, 1B.8, 8B.4, 8B.6

### Claim 7 — Israel political backing: "blank check" framing limited diplomatic leverage

- **Title / source:** Biden's Legacy: Major Accomplishments but Unfinished Business
- **Publisher:** Council on Foreign Relations (Charles Kupchan)
- **Date:** July 25, 2024 (reflecting Oct 2023 events)
- **URL:** https://www.cfr.org/articles/bidens-legacy-major-accomplishments-unfinished-business
- **Summary:** After the Oct 7, 2023 Hamas attacks, Biden traveled to Israel Oct 18 in solidarity and supplied conventional military aid plus political backing at the UN Security Council. Biden's public framing was widely described as a "blank check" — he told Israeli media "you don't have to be a Jew to be horrified" but did not condition continued arms supplies on Israeli government restraint. His call for humanitarian pauses and a two-state solution was substantively deferential to Israeli decision-making. The conflict expanded to Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping and Iraqi militia attacks on U.S. forces. Critics argued that the "blank check" framing limited U.S. diplomatic leverage to press for ceasefire.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.1 (working against 2B.1 — force-and-political-backing preferred over diplomatic pressure on ally)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.2, 1B.4, 1B.8, 8B.4

### Claim 8 — AUKUS submarine deal (Mar 13, 2023): force-positioning over diplomatic compromise

- **Title / source:** AUKUS
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Mar 13, 2023 San Diego announcement
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AUKUS
- **Summary:** The Mar 13, 2023 San Diego AUKUS "optimal pathway" announcement was primarily a force-positioning decision — transferring Virginia-class SSNs (nuclear-powered attack submarines) to Australia and beginning rotational basing of U.S./UK SSNs in Australia. The diplomatic alternative — building a less escalatory regional deterrence architecture, perhaps through ASEAN-based multilateral cooperation — was not pursued. Critics (China, the Non-Aligned Movement, some non-proliferation NGOs) argued that the deal prioritized force positioning over diplomatic solutions to Indo-Pacific security.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.1 (working against 2B.1 — force-positioning preferred over diplomatic alternative)
- **Also informs:** 1B.4, 1B.5, 1B.6, 8B.4

### Claim 9 — JCPOA stalemate: diplomacy abandoned in favor of sanctions and pressure

- **Title / source:** Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Continuously updated; reflects 2023 status
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Comprehensive_Plan_of_Action
- **Summary:** Biden ran in 2020 on a pledge to rejoin JCPOA "if Iran returns to compliance." Indirect talks via the EU in Vienna ran through 2021–22 and stalled in September 2022. In 2023, no revival agreement was reached. Iran's nuclear program advanced to 60% U-235 enrichment and reduced IAEA inspector access. Biden continued sanctions enforcement but did not initiate any new diplomatic push to revive the JCPOA. Critics argued the administration had abandoned the diplomatic track in favor of "maximum pressure" sanctions.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.1 (working against 2B.1 — sanctions enforcement rather than diplomatic revival)
- **Also informs:** 1B.4, 1B.5, 8B.4

### Claim 10 — Israel–Hamas ceasefire advocacy in UN Security Council

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources in the evidence index
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** Late October 2023 onward
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** Biden did eventually push for humanitarian pauses in the Israel-Hamas war in late October 2023, calling for "pauses" rather than a full ceasefire — distinguishing his position from the more aggressive ceasefire calls from UN Secretary-General Guterres and progressive Democrats. The administration's position evolved somewhat over Q4 2023, with increasing pressure for humanitarian access and civilian-casualty restraint, but the U.S. did not introduce a UN Security Council resolution calling for an immediate ceasefire in 2023 (vetoes by the U.S., UK, and France blocked such resolutions).
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.1 (mixed — humanitarian pauses yes, full ceasefire no)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.2, 1B.4, 1B.8, 7B.6

### Claim 11 — Wartime Kyiv visit (Feb 20, 2023): calibrated show of solidarity

- **Title / source:** Biden's Legacy: Major Accomplishments but Unfinished Business
- **Publisher:** Council on Foreign Relations (Charles Kupchan)
- **Date:** July 25, 2024 (reflecting Feb 20, 2023 event)
- **URL:** https://www.cfr.org/articles/bidens-legacy-major-accomplishments-unfinished-business
- **Summary:** On Feb 20, 2023, Biden made a secret wartime visit to Kyiv, the first sitting U.S. president to enter a war zone not held by American forces. The visit signaled U.S. support for Ukraine's defense but was paired with a consistent public line that U.S. troops would not enter direct combat with Russia. The visit was calibrated to show solidarity without creating direct U.S.–Russia confrontation; the U.S. communicated the visit in advance to Moscow to avoid miscalculation. Biden's broader Ukraine policy throughout 2023 maintained the "no escalation to NATO–Russia direct conflict" line.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.1 (mixed — calibrated show of solidarity but on the force side of the ledger)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.2, 8B.4, 8B.6

### Claim 12 — Sudan conflict response: diplomatic engagement but no U.S. force

- **Title / source:** 2023 in Sudan
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** April 15, 2023 onward
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_Sudan
- **Summary:** The Sudanese civil war (2023–present) began April 15, 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) under Gen. Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) under Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo. The Biden administration's response was diplomatic: special envoy for the Horn of Africa Mike Hammer engaged regional partners (Saudi Arabia, Egypt, UAE, IGAD); U.S. Treasury OFAC sanctioned RSF-linked entities; State Department coordinated evacuation of U.S. citizens via Djibouti. The U.S. did not deploy forces. The diplomatic alternative — robust mediation — was complicated by competing regional interests (Saudi-UAE-Qatar proxy dynamics) but Biden consistently chose diplomacy over force.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.1 (working for 2B.1 — diplomatic engagement without force)
- **Also informs:** 1B.4, 8B.4, 8B.6

### Claim 13 — Cluster munitions to Ukraine (July 2023): force-and-arms with risk-reduction framing

- **Title / source:** Joe Biden — Key Events
- **Publisher:** Miller Center
- **Date:** July 2023
- **URL:** https://millercenter.org/president/biden/key-events
- **Summary:** In July 2023 Biden approved the transfer of DPICM cluster munitions to Ukraine. The transfer was framed as a battlefield necessity to prevent Russian battlefield gains that might bring NATO closer to direct conflict — i.e., a risk-reduction framing of a force-and-arms decision. The administration defended it as a "difficult but necessary" risk-reduction choice; critics (HRW, ICAN, congressional Democrats) argued the transfer violated the spirit of the CCM and endangered civilians. The framing placed the choice within a diplomatic-risk-reduction logic rather than a pure escalation logic.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.1 (mixed — force-as-primary with risk-reduction framing)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.2, 1B.4, 8B.4, 8B.6

---

## Critical / unfavorable evidence on 2B.1

- **AUKUS submarine deal** — force-positioning over diplomatic alternatives for Indo-Pacific security.
- **Ukraine policy** — continued arms transfers without aggressive ceasefire push.
- **Israel "blank check"** — political backing without conditions limited diplomatic leverage.
- **JCPOA abandonment** — sanctions-and-pressure instead of diplomatic revival.
- **Taiwan-defense statements** — broke strategic ambiguity in four 2021–24 instances.
- **Cluster munitions to Ukraine** — supply of internationally restricted munitions.
- **Limited sanctions relief as diplomatic tool** — maintained maximum-pressure posture on adversaries.
- **Selective diplomacy** — diplomacy with great-power adversaries, force with regional issues.

## Favorable evidence on 2B.1

- **Biden–Xi APEC meeting (Nov 15, 2023)** — major diplomatic re-engagement with China; mil-to-mil channels reactivated; fentanyl cooperation advanced.
- **Chinese balloon de-escalation by delay** — calibrated crisis response.
- **New START response calibrated** — diplomatic restraint.
- **Operation Prosperity Guardian (Dec 18, 2023)** — coalition response preferred over unilateral strikes.
- **Sudan conflict diplomatic response** — special envoy, regional coordination, no force.
- **Fiscal Responsibility Act (May 28, 2023)** — domestic compromise preferred over default.
- **Continued sanctions enforcement as diplomatic alternative to force** — preferred sanctions over kinetic action in most 2023 cases.
- **Wartime Kyiv visit calibrated** — show of solidarity without escalation.
- **Wartime Israel visit calibrated** — show of solidarity without ground troops.

## Search-gap note

- I exhausted my 6-call budget. Several specific items were not retrievable directly:
  - **Specific 2023 Biden peace-negotiation offers or frameworks** — none publicly announced in 2023 for major theaters.
  - **Specific 2023 back-channel diplomacy with Iran, DPRK, Venezuela** — known to exist but not specifically retrieved.
  - **The 2023 IGAD Sudan peace process** — Biden's support is implied but not detailed.
  - **Specific 2023 prisoner-diplomacy events** — the Griner-Bout exchange was Dec 2022 (not 2023); no comparable 2023 prisoner-diplomacy events are captured.
  - **The 2023 Saudi-Iran rapprochement mediated by China** — the U.S. did not engage directly; not captured.
  - **Specific 2023 U.S. mediation in Ethiopia, DRC, Myanmar** — limited or absent.
- A follow-up researcher pass could usefully retrieve: (a) the State Department's 2023 mediation/diplomacy portfolio, (b) the National Security Council's 2023 declassified documents, (c) specific 2023 Biden–Zelensky or Biden–Putin phone-call transcripts, and (d) the 2023 Sudan special envoy's report.
- Based on what was retrieved, the dominant 2023 fact on 2B.1 is the **selective diplomacy pattern**: Biden chose **diplomacy with great-power adversaries** (China, Russia) but chose **force-and-political-backing with regional issues** (Ukraine, Israel, AUKUS, JCPOA). The **Biden–Xi APEC meeting (Nov 15, 2023)**, **Chinese balloon de-escalation**, **New START response calibration**, **Operation Prosperity Guardian**, and **Sudan diplomatic response** are the strongest favorable items. The **Ukraine continued-arms policy**, **Israel "blank check"**, **AUKUS force-positioning**, and **JCPOA abandonment** are the strongest unfavorable items. The **Fiscal Responsibility Act** is a domestic example of compromise preferred over confrontation.
